Its pricing page lists a Pro tier around $800/month and a custom Enterprise tier; independent reviews have for a while cited a starting point near $3,000/month for enterprise. Either way, you have to book a demo and talk to sales to get a real quote — there's no free trial and no instant signup. intro:
"How much does Evertune cost?" is a frustrating question to research, because Evertune doesn't fully publish its pricing and there's no way to sign up and pay on your own. You book a demo, talk to sales, and get a custom quote — which is normal for enterprise software, but unhelpful when you just want a number.

This page gives you the real, current picture: what Evertune's own pricing page shows, why independent reviews quote a higher starting figure, what you get for the money, and when a free, instant audit is the smarter first move.

sections.heading: The honest answer: there's no single public price
sections.body:
Evertune is sales-gated. There is no transparent price-and-buy page, no free trial, and no self-serve signup — every tier routes you to "Book a demo."

As of 2026, Evertune's own pricing page lists two tiers: a **Pro** plan shown around **$800/month** (roughly 100,000 prompts analyzed, up to ~11 AI models, unlimited brands/competitors/users) and an **Enterprise** plan with **Custom** pricing (unlimited prompts, dedicated CSM, SSO, data-warehouse integrations).

Here's the wrinkle worth knowing: many independent reviews still report Evertune "starting around **$3,000/month**" for a single enterprise tier with no entry plan. That figure is consistent across multiple third-party write-ups and reflects either the Enterprise tier or earlier packaging before the cheaper Pro plan appeared. So both numbers are "true" depending on which tier and which review you read — which is exactly why you can't pin down a price without a sales call. Treat any specific number as an estimate until Evertune quotes you directly.

sections.heading: Why reviewers keep saying '$3,000/month'
sections.body:
The ~$3,000/month framing didn't come from nowhere. Multiple independent reviews — across comparison sites and tool directories — landed on roughly that figure for Evertune's enterprise tier, often with annual contracts, which implies a minimum commitment in the tens of thousands of dollars per year.

That reputation stuck because of what Evertune is built to do. It's an enterprise Generative Engine Optimization platform from ex-Trade Desk founders with around $19M in funding, designed to sample each tracked prompt ~100 times across 10+ AI surfaces — on the order of 1,000,000+ prompts per brand per month — for statistically significant brand metrics. It also layers in consumer-panel data (Evertune cites a very large panel of real user prompts). That depth is genuinely valuable, and it's expensive to run.

The takeaway: if you're evaluating Evertune for an enterprise rollout, budget closer to the higher end and confirm in writing. The newer ~$800 Pro tier lowers the entry point, but it's still demo-gated, so don't assume you can swipe a card and start today.

sections.heading: What you actually get for the money
sections.body:
Evertune is strong where it counts for big brands. For your spend you get high-volume, repeated sampling of AI engines (ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Overviews, Claude, Perplexity, Copilot, Meta AI, DeepSeek), statistically rigorous brand metrics — unaided awareness, share of voice, sentiment, competitive positioning — and CMO-ready reporting. Enterprise adds SSO, dedicated customer success, and warehouse integrations (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, and so on). Logins are unlimited, so whole teams can share one source of truth.

The honest limitation isn't the analytics — it's the gap between insight and execution. Evertune tells you where you stand and why; acting on it still requires content and SEO/GEO work your team has to do. In one cited case, a brand only moved the needle after producing roughly 30,000 words of new authoritative content in-house. So budget for the platform *and* the people who'll act on what it finds. If you don't have an in-house content function, the true cost is higher than the subscription line item.

faqs.q: Does Evertune have a free trial?
faqs.a: No. Evertune does not offer a free trial or a self-serve signup. Every tier, including the lower-cost Pro plan, routes you to "Book a demo," so you'll need a sales conversation to get access and a quote. If you want an instant, no-signup look at your AI visibility first, a free audit tool like AEOeye covers that in minutes.

It depends on the tier. Multiple independent reviews report a starting point around $3,000/month for Evertune's enterprise tier, often on annual contracts. However, Evertune's own pricing page now also lists a Pro tier around $800/month. Both figures circulate because pricing isn't fully transparent — confirm your exact number directly with Evertune.

Evertune is positioned as an enterprise GEO and analytics platform, and like many enterprise tools it uses sales-gated, custom pricing. The Pro tier has a listed price (around $800/month), but the Enterprise tier is "Custom," which is why you'll see different numbers across reviews and why a demo is required for a firm quote.

For large brands that need statistically rigorous AI brand metrics — high-volume prompt sampling, consumer-panel data, competitive share-of-voice, and CMO-ready reporting — Evertune offers genuine depth that lighter tools don't. For small businesses or solo marketers who just want to know if AI recommends them, it's likely overkill; a free instant audit is a better starting point.

It's lighter on enterprise historical dashboards and high-volume statistical sampling than Evertune, but it's the fast, accessible way to see whether AI engines recommend your brand and who's outranking you.
